title: Jealous much?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore jealousy: how it differs from envy, its status as a secondary, self-conscious and anticipatory emotion, and gender differences in sexual versus emotional jealousy (a Penn State study hypothesizing detachment as a defense mechanism). They cover personal and historical factors such as insecurity, height, and past cheating; jealousy in adolescents, friendships and sibling rivalry; romantic jealousy and warning signs of abnormal or neurotic jealousy, including its link to domestic violence; work jealousy; a step-by-step approach to rebuilding broken trust; the old belief that jealousy turns skin green; and animal studies on fairness versus jealousy in dogs and monkeys. The episode closes with listener mail about Mormon polygamy and a sign-off.
topics: apology and making promises after broken trust

segments.title: Opening banter and October awareness months
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a Chuck and Chuck podcast impostor and list October awareness months, then note that jealousy is a recognized trigger of domestic violence, per a 2003 study. Chuck states his opinion that jealousy has no place in healthy relationships, while Josh says small amounts are healthy.

segments.title: Jealousy vs. envy and emotion theory
segments.summary: Envy is wanting something someone else has; jealousy is fear of losing something you already have to someone else. Jealousy is a secondary, self-conscious emotion that requires awareness of others, and Ralph Hoppka describes it as an anticipatory emotion that seeks to prevent loss.

segments.title: Penis envy aside
segments.summary: Chuck raises Freud's concept of penis envy as a side note. The hosts agree it is not about jealousy and that Freud's idea has been largely discarded.

segments.title: Studying jealousy and gender differences
segments.summary: Jealousy is hard to study longitudinally because it is culturally contextual. Women are found to aim jealous anger at the rival and men at the partner, and women may display jealousy more openly. Examples include Fatal Attraction and the Bobbitt case.

segments.title: Sexual versus emotional infidelity
segments.summary: Evolutionary explanations hold that men fear sexual infidelity and women fear emotional betrayal. A Penn State study hypothesized that men who detach from relationships as a defense are more upset by sexual betrayal, which explains why securely committed men may find emotional betrayal worse. Personal history such as past cheating also shapes jealousy.

segments.title: Insecurity, height, and origins of jealousy
segments.summary: A study found that tall men and average-height women were less jealous, while short men and very tall or short women were more so. The hosts conclude that jealousy often stems from insecurity, whether self-generated or caused by someone breaking trust.

segments.title: Adolescent jealousy and friendship jealousy
segments.summary: Children display jealousy over toys and with siblings, and parents are advised to stay out of minor rivalry. A developmental psychology study found lonely or insecure kids are jealous of friendships, and girls were found more jealous than boys among ninth graders. The hosts discuss their own high school experiences.

segments.title: Sibling rivalry and family jealousy
segments.summary: Sibling rivalry is described as a form of family jealousy, and child psychologists advise letting siblings resolve conflicts themselves unless violence occurs, since unconscious side-taking by parents can hurt. Josh and Chuck describe their own sibling relationships.

segments.title: Romantic jealousy and warning signs
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether some jealousy is healthy, with Josh describing a party scenario. They say romantic jealousy is often the first couple fight, and that jealousy becoming abuse is not okay. Warning signs of abnormal jealousy include constant check-ins and checking a partner's phone or address book.

segments.title: Work jealousy
segments.summary: Work jealousy is described as an ugly form competing for the same jobs, promotions, or raises. The hosts say their own rivalry as co-workers is more like sibling rivalry, and they celebrate each other's writing credits.

segments.title: Neurotic jealousy
segments.summary: Abnormal jealousy is also called neurotic, delusional, or morbid jealousy. Causes include insecurity, immaturity, control issues, and broken trust, real or perceived.

segments.title: Rebuilding broken trust
segments.summary: The hosts outline steps for rebuilding broken trust: acknowledge the hurt and take full responsibility, apologize, explain without defending the act, make realistic promises, follow through, and keep an open dialogue. They note rebuilding takes far longer than expected.
topics: apology and making promises after broken trust

segments.title: Green with envy and animal jealousy
segments.summary: The ancient Greeks linked jealousy to bile turning skin green, tied to the four humors. A PNAS study showed dogs and monkeys reacting to unequal treats, but the hosts argue this reflects a sense of fairness rather than jealousy, since animals may lack the self-concept needed for secondary emotions.
topics: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

segments.title: Listener mail on Mormon polygamy
segments.summary: Listener Susan, a Latter-day Saint with polygamous ancestors, clarifies that polygamy was practiced only by a small group of church leaders at the church president's discretion and was discontinued, with excommunication threatened for those who continued. The hosts thank her and mention a Lou Bega email exchange.
topics: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to share National Country Ham Month stories and point to the website's search for more on jealousy and trust.
